JMIR Res Protocols: Authors’ Reply: Accelerometer-Based Step Counts May Be Confounded by Repetitive Motor Behaviors in Adults With Autism Spectrum Disorder

external.description: Dear Editor, We thank the authors for their thoughtful comments regarding our #Protocol paper, Remote Assessment of Physical Function and Physical Activity in Adults With Autism Spectrum Disorder: #Protocol for Feasibility, Validity, and Reliability #Study [1]. We appreciate their interest in the methodological considerations surrounding accelerometer-derived step counts in adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The authors raise an important point regarding the potential influence of repetitive motor behaviors, including stereotypic movements such as hand-flapping, rocking, and pacing, on accelerometer-based step-count estimates. We agree that consumer-grade ##Wearable devices are primarily developed and validated in neurotypical populations and that movement characteristics unique to individuals with ASD may affect measurement accuracy [2, 3]. To our knowledge, there is limited evidence regarding the validity of Fitbit-derived step counts in adults with ASD, particularly among individuals who exhibit prominent repetitive motor behaviors. While prior studies have successfully used Fitbit devices to monitor physical activity and evaluate physical activity interventions in adults with ASD, these studies were not designed to establish the criterion validity of step-count measurement in this population [4, 5]. The purpose of our #Study was to examine the construct validity and test-retest reliability of remotely administered physical function assessments in adults with ASD. Consistent with our analytic framework, Fitbit-derived step counts were included as one of several indicators of physical activity and functioning, alongside measures of lower-extremity function, fall risk, and comorbidity burden, to evaluate the construct validity of patient-reported physical function. Fitbit step counts were not intended to serve as a criterion standard for physical function assessment. We agree that future studies comparing Fitbit-derived step counts with criterion measures such as direct observation, video-coded step counts, or #Research-grade accelerometry in adults with ASD would be valuable, particularly for understanding the potential influence of repetitive motor behaviors on activity-monitoring outcomes. However, such validation was beyond the scope of the current pilot #Study and #Protocol. We appreciate the authors for highlighting this important area for future #Research. Continued investigation into the validity of ##Wearable activity-monitoring technologies in adults with ASD will help strengthen the interpretation and application of physical activity metrics in both #Research and clinical practice. Sincerely, Annabel Nunez-Gaunaurd, PT, PhD on behalf of the authors
external.title: Authors’ Reply: Accelerometer-Based Step Counts May Be Confounded by Repetitive Motor Behaviors in Adults With Autism Spectrum Disorder

record.text: New JMIR MedInform: Deep Learning–Assisted Diagnosis of Middle Ear Diseases in Otoendoscopy Across Clinician Experience Levels: Retrospective Reader Study

external.description: Background: Accurate diagnosis of middle ear diseases remains challenging due to the specialized nature of otoscopic interpretation and the global shortage of otolaryngologists. Objective: We aimed to evaluate the impact of a deep learning–based AI support system on the diagnostic performance of clinicians with varying levels of expertise, specifically focusing on its ability to bridge the gap between trainees and experts. Methods: In this retrospective reader study, a deep learning model (EfficientNet-B4) was developed using a large-scale dataset of 7335 endoscopic images. The model was designed for multi-class classification, simultaneously identifying primary categories (chronic otitis media, otitis media with effusion, or none [indicating the absence of the first two]) and secondary features (attic retraction, myringitis, otomycosis, and ventilation tube). To assess clinical impact, diagnostic performance was compared among 3 otology professors, 5 senior residents, and 5 junior residents using an independent clinical assessment set of 100 images. Participants performed diagnoses both with and without AI-generated predictions, with a time constraint of 1 minute per image to simulate real-world clinical pressure. Results: In 5-fold cross-validation, the deep learning model achieved 94.8% accuracy for the primary classification. The stand-alone AI achieved diagnostic accuracies ranging from 94.0% to 99.0% in the clinical assessment set. external.description: Background: Frailty is a complex syndrome characterized by diminished physiological reserves, resulting in increased vulnerability among older adults. Scalable tools that leverage routinely collected laboratory data could enable earlier risk stratification in aging populations. Objective: The aim of the study is to model frailty risk using Frailty Trait Scale (FTS)-12 scores and biochemical or hematological parameters, and to examine sex-specific patterns in predictors and performance. Methods: This study analyzed data from a population-based cohort of 1485 individuals aged 65 years or older, drawn from the Toledo Study for Healthy Aging (TSHA). Multiple and logistic regression analyses were used to investigate the relationships between biochemical and hematological parameters, and the FTS-12 score. Predictive models were developed separately for female and male participants, incorporating both single and composite risk factors. Model performance was evaluated using correlation coefficients, coefficients of determination, Akaike information criterion, log-likelihood values, and receiver operating characteristic curves, which summarize how well the models distinguish between higher and lower frailty risk.
